I... gosh, I don't really know. I haven't really thought about it. I mean, work is just such a massive part of my day, and it's where all the pressure is, you know? When I clock out and get in my truck to head home, I'm usually just so wiped out from being on my feet all day. So if I do forget something in my personal life, there’s no supervisor there with a clipboard to point it out, and no angry tenants calling the front office to complain about me. I guess I just haven't noticed it. All my energy, every single ounce of it, just goes into trying to keep my head above water at the apartment complex. Well, I mean, I wouldn't say extremely fatigued, not like... not like there's some kind of sickness or something wrong with my actual energy levels, you know? I have normal energy when I'm not physically working myself to the bone. I really think anybody my age doing what I do would feel the exact same way at five o'clock on a Tuesday. So no, I wouldn't call it extreme fatigue at all. Just... just the reality of doing blue-collar maintenance work for a living. It's honest work, but it definitely takes a toll on the joints, so the tiredness makes sense to me.

Well, outside of work... like I said, it's hard to gauge because I live alone and my time off is mostly just recovering. But, you know, if I really think about it, even at work it’s not just the memory thing, like forgetting to call people back. It’s... it’s the actual focusing part, too, which I guess is what you’re asking about. Like, okay, everything is digital now, right? We used to have these pink carbon-copy slips for work orders, and you’d just grab one and go. Now, they’ve got us using these tablets. They gave us all these rugged iPads with thick rubber cases, and every morning I have to log into this portal thing to see my queue. 

And I’ll sit in the cab of my truck, and I’ll open up a digital work order, and I’ll tell myself, "Okay, read the notes, see what Mrs. Higgins needs this time." And I can start reading it, thinking I’ve got it, you know? I’m looking right at the screen, right at the words. But then... I don't know. Halfway through reading the tenant's notes, maybe a landscaper’s leaf blower starts up across the parking lot, or I hear a siren, or my brain just suddenly jumps to the fact that I need to check the inventory on the HVAC filters before noon. And before I know it, I’m staring at the bottom of the screen, and I realize I have absolutely no idea what I just looked at. None. It’s like my eyes scanned the words, but my brain just slipped right off them and went somewhere else entirely. 

And then I have to scroll back up and read it again. Sometimes two or three times. It’s incredibly frustrating because I *want* to read it, I’m *trying* to read it, but it’s like trying to hold onto water. My mind just drifts off to the next noise or the next job on the list. So I guess, yeah, if I’m having that much trouble just reading a paragraph on a screen in my truck where it’s supposed to be quiet, I probably would have trouble concentrating on things at home, too, if I actually tried to sit down and read a book or something. But honestly, by the time I get home, I don't even try to do anything that requires that much mental effort anymore. I just put the TV on because it doesn't matter if I zone out during a commercial or miss half a scene.

Oh, absolutely. The physical part is... well, it's what I've been doing for years, so my hands just kind of know what to do. If I'm under a sink swapping out a P-trap, or I'm replacing a garbage disposal, I've got my wrenches, I've got my bucket, and I'm just working. The physical activity definitely keeps me anchored in the moment, at least for the actual repair itself. 

But here’s the thing, and this is exactly what Dave has been getting so frustrated with me about lately... it’s the follow-through. It’s like the second the physical turning of the wrench is over, my brain just completely checks out of the job. I’ll begin a maintenance job, go in there and do the actual fix—like, say a tenant has a blown breaker and half their kitchen is dark. I’ll go in, find the short, replace the bad outlet, flip the breaker back on, and the lights come on. The physical work is totally done. 

But then... I don't even know how it happens, but I’ll somehow leave all the last steps undone. The non-physical stuff. I’ll pack up my tool bag and just walk out the door. I won't pull out that tablet to close the ticket, or I’ll forget to take my Sharpie out of my pocket and label the electrical panel so the next guy knows which breaker goes to the microwave. Half the time, I don't even check back with the tenant to say, "Hey, you're all set, the power is back." 

I just... I do the hands-on part, and then my mind is already three buildings over, thinking about the next work order, or maybe I'm just distracted by the fact that I need to go grab a bottle of water from the truck. And then Dave will call me two hours later like, "Did you ever fix unit 4B?" And I have to tell him, "Yeah, I did that at 9 AM!" And he'll say, "Well, the ticket is still open in the system and Mrs. Higgins just called the front office asking if anyone is ever coming to tell her if it's safe to plug her fridge back in." 

It is so incredibly embarrassing. I do the hard part, you know? I do the actual physical labor! But because I can't seem to just stand there and focus enough to do the last two minutes of non-physical wrap-up, it looks to the front office like I didn't do the job at all. It’s like I just can't string the whole process together from start to finish once the physical part of the repair is over. My brain just says, "Okay, the pipes aren't leaking, we're done here," and completely drops the ball on everything else.

Like last week, I told Mrs. Higgins I’d come back to check the seal on her window after the sealant dried, and I didn't remember until she called the main office furious. It’s just piled up so much, you know? It's embarrassing. I’ve always prided myself on working hard, but it’s gotten to the point where my supervisor actually sat me down. They told me I needed to come here and get this sorted out because, well, I was in line for a promotion to a supervisory role, and now they’re saying if I don’t get a handle on this, I might lose my shot at moving up entirely. And I just... I can't let that happen. I’ve worked too hard. But no matter how many sticky notes I write or alarms I set, I just keep dropping the ball.\n\nDoctor: Are you experiencing these memory problems in other areas of your life, outside of work?\n\nPatient: I... gosh, I don't really know. I haven't really thought about it. I mean, work is just such a massive part of my day, and it's where all the pressure is, you know? When I clock out and get in my truck to head home, I'm usually just so wiped out from being on my feet all day. I've been doing maintenance for a long time, and at forty-nine, hauling a heavy tool bag up and down three flights of stairs takes a lot more out of you than it did at twenty. So when I get home, I mostly just crash. \n\nThere's not really anyone there to check up on me or tell me if I dropped the ball on something. It's just me at the house. So if I do forget something in my personal life, there’s no supervisor there with a clipboard to point it out, and no angry tenants calling the front office to complain about me. I guess I just haven't noticed it. All my energy, every single ounce of it, just goes into trying to keep my head above water at the apartment complex. Dave—he's my supervisor, the one I mentioned—he's the one who really brought this whole thing to a head. Because before he sat me down, I was just trying to pedal faster, you know? Just trying to outwork the problem, like I always do. So, honestly, outside of work... I really couldn't tell you. I just haven't been paying attention to anything else because the job is what's keeping a roof over my head.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel extremely tired or fatigued when you're not at work?\n\nPatient: Well, I mean, I wouldn't say extremely fatigued, not like... not like there's some kind of sickness or something wrong with my actual energy levels, you know? I'm tired, sure, but it's a normal kind of tired. Like I was saying just a minute ago, I'm forty-nine and I'm hauling around a tool bag that's gotta weigh at least thirty, maybe thirty-five pounds on a good day. And it's not just the stairs at the complex. It's the bending, the kneeling on hard linoleum to snake out a stubborn drain, reaching up for twenty minutes straight to patch a ceiling leak, or wrestling with these ancient window AC units that weigh a ton. \n\nIt's just a very, very physical job. So yeah, when I get home, my feet are barking, my lower back is stiff, and I pretty much just want to drop into my recliner and not move for a few hours. But it's not like I'm completely wiped out for no reason, or like I can't function. Like, on a Saturday, if I have the weekend off and I'm not on call? I'm totally fine. I'll get up at a normal time, make my coffee, maybe run down to the hardware store for my own house projects, or do some yard work. I have normal energy when I'm not physically working myself to the bone. I really think anybody my age doing what I do would feel the exact same way at five o'clock on a Tuesday. It's honest work, but it definitely takes a toll on the joints, so the tiredness makes sense to me.\n\nDoctor: Do you have trouble concentrating or paying attention to tasks outside of work?\n\nPatient: Well, outside of work... like I said, it's hard to gauge because I live alone and my time off is mostly just recovering. But, you know, if I really think about it, even at work it’s not just the memory thing, like forgetting to call people back. It’s... it’s the actual focusing part, too, which I guess is what you’re asking about. Like, okay, everything is digital now, right? We used to have these pink carbon-copy slips for work orders, and you’d just grab one and go. Now, they’ve got us using these tablets. They gave us all these rugged iPads with thick rubber cases, and every morning I have to log into this portal thing to see my queue. \n\nAnd I’ll sit in the cab of my truck, and I’ll open up a digital work order, and I’ll tell myself, \"Okay, read the notes, see what Mrs. Higgins needs this time.\" And I can start reading it, thinking I’ve got it, you know? I have to be, in my line of work. You can't let that stuff get to you, or you'd be miserable. You just have to nod, smile, fix the flapper valve, and move on to the next unit. So I've always been pretty good at just letting things roll off my back. \n\nEven with this whole thing with Dave, my supervisor... I'm not mad at him. I'm not depressed about it. I'm stressed, definitely. Stressed that I might lose my job if I can't figure out how to keep all these balls in the air. But my actual mood? Like, how I feel when I wake up in the morning? It's the same as it's always been. I don't cry for no reason, I don't fly off the handle at people. I'm just... me. Just a very scattered, very stressed-out version of me right now. But no, no real changes in my actual mood, I don't think. Just the normal reactions to feeling like I'm constantly playing catch-up and dropping things left and right.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having any trouble sleeping?\n\nPatient: Sleeping? I mean, my head hits the pillow and I am gone until the alarm goes off at 5:30. \n\nI've always been a pretty solid sleeper, to be fair. Even back when I was younger, working second shift at the bottling plant right out of high school, I could come home at two in the morning and just crash. And it's the same now. Oh, no, no, not at all. It's actually... well, it's kind of the exact opposite of that, really. Headaches? Palpitations like my heart is racing? No, I wouldn't say that. I don't get migraines or feel like I'm having a heart attack or anything. My body feels fine, mostly.

Trouble planning? Organizing? No, honestly, no. That's actually one of the parts of the job I'm best at. I don't have any issue with that at all. 

Every morning, I get in at 7:00 AM, I get my coffee, and I go straight to the breakroom to pull my work orders off the board. And my maintenance cart? It is packed and organized perfectly. I've got my plumbing fittings in one bin, electrical in another, my drywall patch kits tucked in the back where they won't get crushed. I know exactly what I'm doing and how to set it up. I can plan out the whole eight-hour shift down to the minute, even factoring in when certain residents are usually at work so I don't disturb them if I don't have to. 

So the organizing part is completely fine. It's just... it's exactly like I was saying before, it's the follow-through after the task is actually done. The plan itself is beautiful, right up until I finish snaking that drain, pack up my perfectly organized cart, and then completely forget to call the front office to tell them the job is closed out. Dave looks at my daily route and he actually tells me I plan my days better than guys who have been doing this for thirty years. He knows I can organize the work. 

But what good is a perfect plan if I walk away and leave the priority ticket sitting on a tenant's kitchen counter? So, no, the planning and the organizing aren't the issue at all. My brain handles that part just fine. It's just the remembering everything else that's ruining my shot at this lead position.

Breakfast? Oh, wow. Um... let me think about that. 

See, my mornings are usually pretty much the exact same routine, because if I don't stick to the routine, I end up running late. I get up at 5:30, right? I let the dog out, I start the coffee maker—I have one of those programmable ones, but half the time I forget to set it the night before, so I just stand there in the dark waiting for it to brew. And this morning... well, this morning I was already stressing about that HVAC vendor I mentioned earlier, because I knew I needed to catch him before he sent his guys out to the wrong building.

It’s terrible, isn't it? My brain was just already at work, already panicking about Dave and my backlog and the safety review, so that whole hour before I actually clocked in is just a complete blur. So, honestly? No, I really don't know what I had for breakfast.

I'll look right at a tenant, tell them I'm going to do something, and then it's just gone from my head. \n\nAnd it’s piled up so much lately, just one dropped ball after another, that work actually sent me here. They literally told me I had to come get this figured out before I lose my shot at moving up to that lead maintenance job. So, you know, my apartment being a little messy because I forgot to run the vacuum or wipe down the counters? I can live with that. I live alone, nobody cares. But losing my chance at a promotion and a company truck because I can't remember to follow up on a simple work order? That's what I can't handle. That's why I'm here.\n\nDoctor: Do you find it harder to remember instructions or follow through with tasks when you're doing something physical at the same time?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, no, not at all. It's actually... well, it's kind of the exact opposite of that, really. Like I was trying to explain before with the plumbing and the electrical jobs, the physical part is actually my safe zone. When my hands are busy, it's like... I don't know, it's like my brain is finally quiet for a second. If Dave—my supervisor, you know—if he walks up to me while I'm actively snaking a drain, right? And I'm physically feeding the auger cable down the pipe, and he starts rattling off a list of instructions for what he needs me to do next, I can actually hear him better. It's like the physical movement takes up just enough of that restless energy in my head that the rest of my brain can actually tune in to what he's saying. \n\nBut if I'm just standing still? If I'm sitting in the breakroom staring at a coffee cup and he gives me those exact same instructions? Forget about it. It just goes in one ear and out the other. So no, doing something physical doesn't make it harder to remember things at all. It honestly helps me. \n\nIt's always that moment right *after* the physical part stops that the trouble starts. That's the real danger zone for me. The second the wrench goes back in the tool bag, the instructions just vanish. And, you know, like I keep saying, that's what's absolutely killing my chances at this lead position. I mean, I'm forty-nine years old, I've been doing this forever, and I'm finally looking at a real, actual promotion with a company truck, and it all hinges on the fact that I can't seem to hold onto a thought unless my hands are covered in grease or drywall dust. It just makes me so mad at myself, because the physical work is great, I'm really good at it, but the rest of it... it's just slipping right through my fingers the second I stop moving.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever experience any physical sensations, like headaches or palpitations, when you realize you've forgotten something or can't focus?\n\nPatient: Headaches? Palpitations like my heart is racing? No, I wouldn't say that. I don't get migraines or feel like I'm having a heart attack or anything. My body feels fine, mostly. \n\nIt's more of a... well, it's like a massive, heavy drop in my gut. You know that feeling when you reach into your pocket for your wallet and it's not there? Or when you step off a curb you didn't realize was there? That sudden, cold sinking feeling in your stomach? That's exactly what it is. It's not a medical palpitation, it's just pure, absolute dread. \n\nBecause every single time it happens, every time I'm walking across the courtyard and it suddenly hits me that I forgot to call the HVAC vendor back, or I left a priority work order sitting on the breakroom table... my brain immediately goes straight to Dave and that promotion. There goes the company truck.\" \n\nI don't get a headache, I just get so incredibly frustrated with myself. I mean, I just want to crawl under a sink and stay there. I'm forty-nine years old, I've been working with my hands my whole life, and I should be able to remember to make a simple five-minute phone call without feeling like my whole career is crashing down around me. So, physically? No, no actual headaches or anything like that. It's just that awful, terrible realization that I'm sabotaging my one good shot at moving up, and I just can't seem to stop doing it.\n\nDoctor: Do you have trouble planning out your day or organizing your tasks?\n\nPatient: Trouble planning? Organizing? No, honestly, no. That's actually one of the parts of the job I'm best at. I don't have any issue with that at all. \n\nEvery morning, I get in at 7:00 AM, I get my coffee, and I go straight to the breakroom to pull my work orders off the board. And I can look at that stack of papers and just map out the entire day in my head perfectly. I'll organize them by building—you know, so I'm not dragging my tools all the way from Building 2 down to Building 12 and then dragging them all the way back up to Building 4. I put them in a totally logical order. I'll say, okay, we've got a leaky P-trap over here, a jammed garbage disposal there, and a busted ceiling fan in the clubhouse. \n\nAnd my maintenance cart? I know exactly what I'm doing and how to set it up. Fewer distractions? Gosh, I... I don't even know how to answer that, to be perfectly honest with you. Because, see, my whole job is just one giant distraction. I don't think I've ever had a day in the last four years where there weren't a million things flying at me all at once. 

Like, just to give you an idea of what I deal with—picture this. I’m in unit 4B, right? I’ve got my head shoved under the kitchen sink trying to swap out a burnt-out garbage disposal, trying to remember if I grabbed the right size wire nuts from the shop. And right at that exact second, my radio starts squawking at full volume. It’s Dave, asking if I ever got around to checking the pool chemicals. So I pull my head out from under the sink, I reach for my radio to answer him, and while I'm holding down the button, the tenant in 4B taps me on the shoulder to ask if I can also look at her sliding glass door because it's sticking on the track. And while *that* is happening, my cell phone is vibrating in my cargo pocket because the supply house is texting me about a backordered part for a completely different job. 

It’s just... it's constant. It never stops. So, would I remember things better if all of that went away? If it was just me and one single task in a quiet room? I mean... maybe? I really, truly don't know. I've never actually had a quiet day at work to test that theory out on! 

And the thing is, even when I *am* by myself—like at the end of the day when everybody else has gone home and I'm just sitting alone in the maintenance shop at my little metal desk, supposedly with zero distractions, just trying to close out my work orders on the computer... I still can't seem to get it done. It'll be dead quiet in there, just the hum of the vending machine in the corner, and I'll still somehow end up realizing I've spent the last twenty minutes reorganizing the drill bits by size instead of logging my hours. Or I'll get up to throw away a coffee cup and end up sweeping the entire shop floor, and completely forget I was in the middle of ordering air filters. 

So it’s like... sure, the property is loud and crazy, but sometimes I feel like I don't even need outside distractions to lose my train of thought. I can derail myself just fine in a completely empty room. So, honestly? I really couldn't tell you if fewer distractions would fix my memory. I’d like to think it would help, but I just don't know for sure.
